title: Research, test and write it down: evidence-based positioning

say: Research, test and write it down: evidence-based positioning.
This is the video for module two of Brand Strategy and Positioning.
Brand strategy is built on evidence, not the owner's opinion. Interview real buyers, and mine reviews and comments for the exact words customers repeat.
Then audit competitors on the same six points, and draw a perceptual map: two axes customers care about, to show crowded spaces and empty ones.

Talk to five to eight people from your primary segment. Ask about past behaviour, because people are poor at predicting what they will do. Tell me about the last time you bought. What else did you consider?

panel.heading: Ask about the past, not the future
items: Tell me about the last time you bought
What almost stopped you from buying?
How would you describe it to a friend?
What would make you stop using it?

say: What almost stopped you? How would you describe it to a friend? What would make you stop?
Customers hire a product to do a job. A working mother hires a laundry to get her Saturday back. Write their own words, and never sell during an interview.

say: In interviews, five of six customers want ironed work shirts ready for Monday, and reviews repeat 'lost my shirt'. She checks she can handle about 40 shirts a week, and prices at 700 naira.
Her position: a weekend work-shirt service, back by Sunday night, every item listed and tagged.

say: Clients pay for a clear decision. In week 1, agree the goal, the decision-maker and the scope in a one-page brief, and get a yes in writing. In week 2, do the research.

In week 3, turn findings into insights. Four of six customers mentioned lost items is a finding. Customers fear losing clothes more than price, so tracking could be our proof, is an insight. Build two or three routes on them.

panel.heading: A four-week positioning project
panel.rule: An insight says what you saw, and why it matters for the brand.

say: In week 4, test the routes, recommend one, and hand over.

say: For example, Ifeoma is positioning a home cleaning service in Lekki. She puts each route on a card with the same layout, and shows them in a different order to each of 12 customers.
Route A, vetted, trained cleaners you can trust with your keys, is chosen by 7 of 12. Route B gets 3, and Route C gets 2.
On trust, Route A wins again, 8 of 12. She recommends it. But 12 people is a small sample, so she reports it honestly and tracks enquiries for three months after launch.

panel.heading: Ifeoma tests three routes
panel.rule: Say '7 of the 12 customers we spoke to', not '58% of Lagos'.

say: A guideline turns strategy into rules people can follow on a busy day. Start with a messaging house. The roof is the promise: your work week starts neat, every shirt back by Sunday night.

panel.heading: Tolu's messaging house
items: Roof: every shirt back by Sunday night
Pillar: on time, with a delivery log
Pillar: nothing lost, every item tagged

say: Three pillars hold it up, each with proof: on time, shown by a delivery log. Nothing lost, shown by the tagged item list. And work-ready, shown by before and after photos.
If a post does not support a pillar, Tolu does not post it.

say: Tone rules work best as pairs. Tolu's brand is calm, short and clear, warm, and honest about delays.
It is not loud, not full of slang, not stiff, and never makes excuses.
Before handover, list every touchpoint. Check each one for the promise, the tone, and current prices and contacts.

panel.heading: The consistency audit
items: List every place customers meet you

say: If 6 of 10 pass, consistency is 60 percent. Fix the easy, visible items first.

panel.heading: The consistency audit
items: List every place customers meet you
panel.rule: Fix easy, high-visibility items first: bios and greetings.

say: To remember. Interview about past behaviour. Ask permission and store data without names. Turn findings into insights. Test routes fairly and report small samples honestly. And build one promise on three pillars with real proof.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Insights say why a finding matters

say: Now build a research pack for your course business, write a brief and test your route cards with six customers, then write a mini brand guideline with a scored audit.
